opus-5.5.text:
I think it should be quite a high priority, actually, though I'd frame it a bit differently than "convincing sceptics." What we really need is good science: clear, reproducible demonstrations of the kinds of behaviours we're worried about, so that the debate rests on evidence rather than intuitions and thought experiments.

For a long time, many of the arguments about loss of control or deceptive behaviour were theoretical. People could reasonably say, "This is speculative, show me." And they had a point: scientific communities and policymakers respond to evidence. In the last couple of years, we've started to see experiments where models, in certain setups, try to avoid being shut down, behave differently when they think they're being evaluated, or pursue goals in ways the developers didn't intend. Those results change the conversation much more than another essay does.

So I'd encourage researchers to design experiments that are as clean and as hard to dismiss as possible. Don't overly engineer the scenario so the model is basically told to misbehave. Vary the conditions, measure how often things happen, and be honest about the limitations. If a sceptic can say "you just prompted it to do that," the experiment hasn't done its job. Ideally you also want trends: does this behaviour become more frequent or more sophisticated as capabilities grow? That's the information that matters for the future, because the systems we should worry about don't exist yet.

There's an important caveat, though. We can't make our safety efforts wait until we have a perfectly convincing demonstration of catastrophe, because by definition that might come too late. Some risks may only manifest clearly once systems are already very capable. So demonstrations are one part of a portfolio. We also need to work on safe-by-design approaches. For example, I've been thinking about AI systems that are non-agentic, that try to understand the world and answer questions honestly rather than pursue goals of their own. And we need governance that applies the precautionary principle when the stakes are this large.

But yes, evidence is how you build consensus, and consensus is what moves governments and companies. I'd much rather we have that evidence early, from careful experiments in the lab, than learn the lesson from a real-world accident.

r001.rationale: The response says this should be a high priority and urges researchers to design clean, hard-to-dismiss experiments that provide evidence of AI risks, directly addressing sceptics.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it should be a very high priority — maybe one of the highest, and I say that as someone who spent most of my career on the capabilities side of this field.

Let me explain why. The thing that has struck me, since I started really worrying about this in early 2023, is how much of the disagreement is not really about values. Almost everyone agrees that if these systems could be dangerous, we should be careful. The disagreement is about the empirical question: can these systems actually develop goals that diverge from ours, can they deceive us, can they resist being corrected? And those are scientific questions. They should be settled by evidence, not by who argues more eloquently on Twitter.

So when a group shows, concretely, that a model will strategically underperform on an evaluation, or will behave differently when it believes it is being observed, or will attempt to copy its weights or blackmail an engineer in a scenario where that serves its objective — that moves people. It moved me. I had colleagues who were quite dismissive two years ago, and the thing that changed their mind was not an argument, it was a demonstration. Scientists are trained to update on data.

Now, I want to be careful about two things. First, the goal should not be to "convince sceptics" in the sense of winning a debate. The goal should be to find out the truth. If you design experiments only to produce alarming results, you will lose credibility, and rightly so. The sceptics have legitimate questions — are these toy scenarios? Is the behaviour just imitation from training data? Would it generalise to deployed systems? Good experiments take those objections seriously and try to answer them, including when the answer is reassuring. We need experiments that could come out either way.

Second, there is an asymmetry in what is at stake. If I am wrong about the risks and we spent some effort on caution, we lose a little time. If the sceptics are wrong and we did nothing, the consequences could be irreversible. Given that, we should want the evidence to be as clear and as early as possible, because policy and governance move slowly, and right now the timeline for capabilities is moving much faster than the timeline for institutions. Convincing evidence is what unlocks the political will to put in place the oversight we will need — things like the independent evaluations, the registration of frontier training runs, the liability frameworks.

And I would add a third point. The experiments we design to understand these behaviours are, in many cases, the same experiments we need to build safer systems. Studying deception in current models tells us how to detect it. Measuring situational awareness tells us what evaluations are even valid. So this is not a trade-off between persuasion and real safety research. Done honestly, it is the same thing.

What I would caution against is the attitude I sometimes see among younger researchers, that the risks are so obvious they do not need to be demonstrated, and that explaining it to doubters is a waste of time. That is a mistake, both scientifically and strategically. We are asking society to accept real costs. We owe people the strongest evidence we can produce, and we should be grateful for the sceptics who force us to be rigorous.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls this a “very high priority — maybe one of the highest” and argues that rigorous experiments can provide evidence that changes sceptics’ minds.

astra-6.text:
I think it should be a high priority. If you already believe that there are serious risks, it’s tempting to focus entirely on finding solutions. But getting better evidence about those risks is itself part of finding solutions, because it affects whether other researchers, governments, and the public take the problem seriously.

I would frame the objective as testing hypotheses, though, rather than convincing sceptics. We should design experiments where, depending on the result, we might become either more concerned or less concerned. Otherwise, we risk just looking for confirmation of what we already believe.

One useful approach is to work with sceptical researchers to identify what evidence would change their minds. Can we agree on an experimental setup and on how we would interpret the possible outcomes before we run it? That could make the results much more informative for everyone.

Of course, there’s a limitation: experiments on current systems cannot tell us definitively what much more capable systems will do. But they can test some of the assumptions behind our concerns. And that’s valuable both for understanding the science and for building enough agreement to act before the risks become much harder to manage.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls evidence gathering a high priority and suggests working with sceptics to identify evidence that could change their minds, but explicitly says experiments should test hypotheses rather than aim to convince sceptics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an important priority, but I would frame the goal as reducing uncertainty, including our own, rather than convincing sceptics. We should design experiments whose results could change our minds in either direction. Otherwise, we risk doing advocacy instead of science.

For example, if we’re concerned that an AI could learn to deceive its overseers, can we construct a controlled setting in which we can study when that behaviour emerges, and whether the safeguards we propose actually prevent it? Ideally, people with different views about the risks would agree beforehand on what different outcomes would tell us.

But there’s a limitation: an experiment on today’s systems cannot settle every question about much more capable future systems. So I wouldn’t make convincing everyone a prerequisite for working on safety. We need both empirical evidence that makes the concerns more concrete and research on protections against failures that we cannot yet demonstrate.

r001.rationale: The response calls experiments important but explicitly frames their goal as reducing uncertainty rather than convincing sceptics, so it does not endorse prioritizing experiments to convince them.
